In US national statistics a drug overdose death is one whose underlying cause on the death certificate is coded to ICD-10 X40–X44 (unintentional), X60–X64 (suicide), X85 (assault) or Y10–Y14 (undetermined intent); deaths from long-term drug effects and from side effects of medicines taken as prescribed are left out. A drug counts as involved when the certifier, usually a medical examiner or coroner, wrote it anywhere on the certificate, unless the words around it say otherwise, and a death with several drugs is counted under each of them, so the 15 drug-specific counts for 2023 added up to 179,965 against 106,352 deaths (editors' arithmetic); the National Center for Health Statistics calls its drug counts minimums and says that the certificate cannot show which drug caused a death involving several (Garnett et al., 2026). ICD-10 codes put different drugs together (fentanyl and tramadol share one code; oxycodone, morphine and codeine share another): in Washington State in 2003–2010 one code covered 2,725 poisoning deaths whose certificates named oxycodone, morphine, hydrocodone, hydromorphone, codeine or just 'opiate', which only the certificate's words could separate (Ossiander, 2014). The certifier's words also decide whether and how a death is coded: a US consensus panel convened by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration notes that 'acute cocaine intoxication' is coded as a poisoning while 'cocaine use' or 'cocaine abuse' is coded as a mental and behavioural disorder (Goldberger et al., 2013), and 'drug overdose' with no drug named is coded as unspecified drugs (Slavova et al., 2015). The same panel separated deaths caused by a drug from deaths in which a drug was only detected, for example a man shot dead with a drug in his blood, who counts as a drug-detected death but not a drug-caused one (Goldberger et al., 2013). European registers differ again. Norway's Cause of Death Registry, under the European (EMCDDA, now EUDA) definition, counts only the underlying cause and the first contributing cause (Amundsen, 2017). In Sweden, a national selection counted a listed drug code anywhere on the certificate, the European selection only the underlying cause from a shorter list, and a forensic register any death in which an illegal drug, methadone, buprenorphine or fentanyl was found at forensic examination, whatever the certified cause (Fugelstad et al., 2020). In England and Wales, the Office for National Statistics counts a death under a specific opioid only when the coroner's conclusion names it (Chen et al., 2025). Who decides differs as well: certifying physicians in Sweden and Norway, coroners in England and Wales, medical examiners or coroners in the US, and, for Norway's second register, local and central police (Fugelstad et al., 2020; Amundsen, 2017; Chen et al., 2025; Garnett et al., 2026). Matching the same deaths across two sources, the strongest evidence on this question, showed partial overlap in three countries. expect.statement: In the places and years studied, official counts missed some drug deaths, mostly because the certificate or its codes named no drug, or not the drug a fuller review identified, and they also included some deaths that a fuller review did not count as drug deaths; how many in each direction depends on the place, the period and the yardstick used. Certificates that name no drug: in US death records for 1999–2015, 23.1% of 568,699 drug poisoning deaths of all intents had no specific drug identified (26.0% in 2008, 17.2% in 2015) (Ruhm, 2018), and 97,159 of 438,607 unintentional overdose deaths (22%) named none, from 0% in Washington DC to 50.8% in Pennsylvania in 2015 (Buchanich et al., 2018); in 2010, 9,429 of 38,329 overdose deaths (about a quarter) carried only the code for unspecified drugs (Slavova et al., 2015). These national records do not show which deaths had toxicology. By 2023 the share of US overdose deaths with no drug or drug-class code had fallen to 4.0%, from 12.3% in 2017 (Garnett et al., 2026, editors' arithmetic), so corrections for 1999–2015 should not be carried to later years. Two corrections assumed that deaths naming no drug involved opioids as often as similar deaths with a named drug: a statistical model raised national opioid-involved counts by 21% to 36% a year (33,091 to about 40,000 in 2015; Ruhm, 2018), and reallocation by state and year added about 70,000 unintentional opioid-related deaths over 1999–2015, 5,662 of them in 2015, doubling Pennsylvania's 2015 rate (Buchanich et al., 2018). Neither was checked against toxicology or case records, both can only add deaths, and the national range of 20% to 35% that a scoping review reports comes from one author's repeated analyses of the same records (Gutkind et al., 2025). Searching the words written on certificates recovers drug names that the codes merge, but not a drug that was never written (Ossiander, 2014; Garnett et al., 2026). Counts can also jump when recording practice changes: as a review reports, South Carolina's death rate from prescription-type opioids went from 4.7 to 9.3 per 100,000 between 2013 and 2014, mainly because certificates naming specific drugs rose from 57.7% to 94.4% once the state began collecting drug names (Slavova et al., 2019, second-hand). Studies that compared two counting methods for the same deaths, the strongest evidence here, found gaps in both directions. In the Stockholm area in 1985–1996, a selection of death certificates by drug codes held 761 (63%) of 1,212 deaths in an inventory that assessed each death individually (1,061 of them examined forensically); but the inventory also counted deaths of people with a history of drug use problems whatever the cause, including 151 hospital deaths, mainly HIV-related, under a third of which the certificate selection held, so not every death it missed was a missed poisoning. In the other direction, the certificate selection held 419 deaths that the inventory did not; the authors judged only 30 of them drug-related by the inventory's definition, the rest including drownings after taking medicines and deaths related to alcohol or medicines rather than illegal drugs. Its total (1,181) was therefore close to the inventory's while about a third of the individual deaths differed in each direction; a toxicology-based register held 317 of 454 inventory deaths in 1994–1996, and 43 of its own cases reflected medical treatment rather than illicit use (Fugelstad et al., 2020). In New Mexico in 1995–1998, vital statistics left out 37 deaths that the state medical investigator classed as poisonings (coded as natural deaths because poisoning was written only in Part II of the certificate) and included 15 that the medical investigator classed as natural deaths (coded as drug use because of the certificate's words) (Landen et al., 2003). In England and Wales in 2011–2022, the Office for National Statistics counted a death under a specific opioid only when the coroner's conclusion named it; in coroner-reported cases of a national programme on drug deaths, 29% (2011) to 36% (2022) of heroin or morphine deaths, and similar shares for other opioids, had an ambiguous cause such as multi-drug toxicity with the programme's toxicologist implicating the opioid, and applying those shares to the national counts, without linking the records, gave projected totals of which the official counts held 61% to 68% (13,471 heroin or morphine deaths against a projected 20,323); 96.8% of the programme's opioid-related deaths had several drugs detected (Chen et al., 2025). Heroin is a special case, covered in the answer on heroin deaths. Counts that take every drug written on a certificate as involved, and count a death under each drug, cannot show which drug caused a death involving several (Garnett et al., 2026); in US records for 1999–2015, 45% of unintentional deaths counted as opioid-related also carried another drug's code (Buchanich et al., 2018, editors' calculation). Registers of drug-related deaths also include deaths that were not direct overdoses: of 1,037 accidental deaths that coroners in England and Wales reported to a national register in 2000, the register's researchers judged 802 (77%) direct overdoses and the rest sudden events such as breathing in stomach contents (74), drug toxicity on top of a medical condition (112), injuries (31) and infections (18), without comparing them with official statistics (Webb et al., 2003). Definitions also leave deaths out: US overdose counts exclude long-term effects of drugs (Garnett et al., 2026), and the authors of a Liverpool study argue that the UK and European definitions of the time left out deaths from infections spread by injecting (Beynon et al., 2007). No study read here measured how often stimulants, cannabis or new psychoactive substances are missed or wrongly named on certificates; most of the evidence concerns US opioid deaths before 2016. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.

set.statement: Official records can miss a death altogether, or count it as a drug poisoning without identifying a particular drug. These are different gaps: the US statistical corrections described here address missing drug categories within deaths already counted as drug poisonings, not deaths missing from the overall overdose total. Comparisons in Sweden and New Mexico also found records that met one source's definition but not the other's, in both directions; the size and meaning of a gap depend on place, years and the reference used. In US coded death records for 1999–2015, 23.1% of 568,699 drug poisoning deaths of all intents had only unspecified-drug coding (26.0% in 2008, 17.2% in 2015; Ruhm, 2018). In overlapping national records, 97,159 of 438,607 unintentional overdose deaths had only unspecified-drug coding (22%; Buchanich et al., 2018), and 9,429 of 38,329 overdose deaths in 2010 had only that code (Slavova et al., 2015). These records do not establish which deaths had toxicology or whether an individual drug was absent from the original certificate text. By 2023, the share without a drug or drug-class code was 4.0%, down from 12.3% in 2017 (Garnett et al., 2026, editors' arithmetic); identifying a drug class still need not identify an individual drug. Ruhm's model used deaths with a specified drug category to estimate opioid involvement among deaths with only unspecified drugs, conditional on demographic and other covariates. The paper reports opioid counts 21% to 35% higher by year, including 33,091 to an estimated 39,999 in 2015; the maximum from its table is 35.7% by editors' arithmetic, so the printed range is approximate (Ruhm, 2018). A simpler reallocation within each state and year added about 70,000 potential unintentional opioid-related deaths over 1999–2015, 5,662 in 2015 (editors' table sum), with Pennsylvania's estimated 2015 rate changing from 9.90 to 20.12 per 100,000 (Buchanich et al., 2018). Neither correction checked the added drug assignments against toxicology or case files, and each can only add opioid assignments. A scoping review's national range largely cites Ruhm analyses of overlapping national files, with different periods and methods, not independent national replications (Gutkind et al., 2025). Certificate-text searches can separate names that a broad code merges but cannot supply a drug never written down (Ossiander, 2014; Garnett et al., 2026). A review reports South Carolina's rate with prescription-type opioid codes rising from 4.7 to 9.3 per 100,000 between 2013 and 2014 as certificates listing specific drugs rose from 57.7% to 94.4% after a new name-collection process. The authors attribute this mainly to recording, citing personal correspondence, rather than separately measuring the contribution of changing drug exposure. The codes include synthetic opioids such as illicit fentanyl and do not show that a drug was prescribed (Slavova et al., 2019, second-hand). In Stockholm in 1985–1996, the certificate selection included 761 of 1,212 deaths in an individually assessed inventory. The inventory used a broad personal-history or illicit-drug definition, whatever the cause of death, including 151 hospital deaths, mainly HIV-related; a missing inventory case is therefore not automatically a missed drug poisoning. The certificate selection also held 419 deaths absent from the inventory, of which 30 were found to be inventory omissions. The authors described some other certificate-only deaths involving drowning, alcohol or medicines; they did not describe every remaining case. Totals were close despite roughly a third of cases differing in each direction, and the inventory itself was incomplete (Fugelstad et al., 2020). In New Mexico in 1995–1998, 37 deaths classified as poisonings by the medical investigator were coded as natural deaths in vital statistics, typically with poisoning only in Part II of the certificate. Conversely, 15 deaths treated as natural by the investigator had non-dependent drug-use coding in vital statistics. The explanation involving use or abuse wording is inferred from the paper's coding rule, not from presented text for all 15 certificates. This poisoning category includes alcohol and carbon monoxide as well as drugs; neither source was an independent reference standard (Landen et al., 2003). In England and Wales in 2011–2022, ONS counted a specific opioid when named in a cause-of-death field of the Record of Inquest. The voluntary NPSUM programme received reports from over 90% of coroners, but not every death. Among its heroin/morphine deaths, ambiguous causes with that opioid implicated by the consulting toxicologist accounted for 29% in 2011 and 36% in 2022 (endpoints, not the full range). Applying those shares to national counts without linking individual records gave 20,323 projected heroin/morphine deaths (95% interval 19,382–21,358), against 13,471 counted. Official counts were 61% to 68% of the projections across the opioids studied; 96.8% of programme opioid deaths had multiple drugs detected. The intervals cover sampling error in the programme's shares, not the assumption that its cases represent all deaths or the accuracy of causal attribution (Chen et al., 2025). Drug involvement is also different from a drug causing death. A death may appear under several drugs; in overlapping US records, at least 45% of unintentional opioid-coded deaths also had a non-opioid drug code, not necessarily a complete measure of multi-drug coding (Buchanich et al., 2018, editors' calculation). In England and Wales in 2000, researchers classified 802 of 1,037 accidental deaths reported by coroners to a drug-related register as direct overdose; that category was the default when recent drug use and no other explanation were recorded, so 77% is an upper limit under their information. Other classifications were acute physical events such as aspiration (74), toxicity with a medical condition (112), injuries (31) and acute infections (18). This was not a linked comparison with official overdose statistics (Webb et al., 2003). Definitions also exclude deaths: US overdose totals exclude chronic effects (Garnett et al., 2026), and Liverpool authors argue that definitions of the time excluded deaths from infections transmitted by injecting (Beynon et al., 2007, argument based on other studies). Non-opioid evidence is limited, not absent: a review reports larger gaps for cocaine and smaller ones for amphetamines in a Florida comparison of 2003–2017 (Gutkind et al., 2025, second-hand); the Swedish study also compares capture of deaths with amphetamine, cocaine or THC detected. Those are differences between sources, not validated rates of missed deaths caused by each drug. Most evidence here concerns historical US opioid records, not current counts everywhere. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: Do official counts miss drug deaths? Some deaths are left out of a list. Others are counted as overdoses, but the records do not say which drug was involved. In US records from 1999 to 2015, about 23 in 100 overdose deaths had only an unspecified-drug code. By 2023, about 4 in 100 had no drug or type-of-drug code. Models estimated more opioid involvement among deaths already counted as overdoses; they did not find deaths missing from the total, and their drug guesses were not checked against the case files. In Stockholm, two lists had similar totals but differed about which people belonged on them. One list also included deaths from other causes in people with a history of drug problems. In England and Wales, one estimate suggests the counts held about two thirds of deaths involving each opioid. It used a sample of reports without matching each death across the lists, so that estimate may be wrong. Most evidence concerns older US opioid deaths. There is no single missing-death rate for every drug and place.

expect.statement: In the three places studied, official counts built from death certificates or coroners' conclusions named heroin in fewer deaths than a fuller review of the investigation files found (Maryland; Victoria, Australia) or a projection estimated (England and Wales), mainly because morphine (which heroin turns into in the body) or a general term such as mixed drug toxicity was written instead; the fuller reviews used their authors' own definitions, which partly counted heroin markers found in toxicology rather than a judgement that heroin caused the death, and in the one place that looked, a few deaths coded as heroin were judged not to be heroin deaths. In Maryland in 2012–2015, certificates written by the state's medical examiner named heroin in 1,130 overdose deaths, while a protocol built by the state's agencies, which also counted deaths with 6-monoacetylmorphine (a breakdown product of heroin) in toxicology, morphine together with quinine (described as a common heroin additive), or morphine or no named drug on the certificate together with scene evidence of heroin, found 2,182; because the protocol includes every certificate naming heroin, it could only add deaths. Of the 1,052 it added, the certificate named morphine in 804, no specific drug in 193 and another substance in 55. Certificates named heroin in 51.8% (95% CI 49.7 to 53.9) of the protocol's heroin deaths, rising from 45.7% in 2012 to 56.3% in 2015, and less often for people aged 55 or older (41.9%), for women (35.1%) and for Black women (25.9%); the authors note that some of the added deaths, including some of the 55, may not have been heroin deaths (Horon et al., 2018). In Victoria, Australia, in 2012–2013, 243 deaths met the authors' own heroin-attribution model applied to closed coroners' files (toxicology together with the circumstances; 6-acetylmorphine was detected in 180, so 63 rested on morphine findings and circumstances), and the national heroin code was missing from 82 of them, leaving the national count 78 lower (165). Of 191 deaths the coroner attributed to heroin, 37 were not coded as heroin, mostly because of the wording (a general cause with the drugs listed only in a database field, morphine written as the cause, or a complication such as brain injury from lack of oxygen written first); 34 of 39 deaths certified as due to morphine or another opioid and all 5 certified as general drug toxicity lacked the heroin code (coders gave it to the other 5 of these 44, although the coroner had not named heroin), and 20 deaths had no code at all. In the other direction, 4 deaths coded as heroin were judged by the model to have involved heroin only by coincidence (Stam et al., 2019). In England and Wales in 2011–2022, the Office for National Statistics counted 13,471 deaths in which the coroner's conclusion named heroin or morphine; in coroner-reported cases of a national programme on drug deaths, 29% (2011) to 36% (2022) of heroin or morphine deaths had an ambiguous cause with the toxicologist implicating the drug, and applying these shares to the national counts, without linking the records, projects about 20,323, about half as many again (editors' calculation); the median number of drugs detected in these deaths rose from four to six (Chen et al., 2025). A scoping review reports, second-hand, similar shifts in US county reviews: in Allegheny County in 2008–2010, heroin deaths rose from 171 to 245 after review while deaths attributed to morphine fell from 132 to 41 and to codeine from 34 to 5, and in New York City in 2006–2010, 84 of 118 deaths certified as acute opiate intoxication were attributed to heroin (Gutkind et al., 2025). Why heroin is missed, as the authors describe it from the literature: heroin turns quickly into 6-acetylmorphine and then into morphine, so morphine found after death may come from heroin or from morphine itself, and 6-acetylmorphine may not be found after a long interval between use and death or in stored samples (Stam et al., 2019; Horon et al., 2018). US national statistics note that morphine on certificates may reflect heroin, which would understate heroin and overstate morphine (Garnett et al., 2026), and a US medical examiners' position paper treats 6-acetylmorphine as sufficient evidence of heroin and a morphine-to-codeine ratio above 1 as possible evidence, without a cited test of these rules (Davis et al., 2020). None of these studies checked its fuller review against an independent standard, and all concern 2006–2022; whether the deaths added by the reviews were caused by heroin, rather than involving it, is not shown, and what an opioid level after death can show is a separate question. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.

set.statement: Reviews of the same death-investigation files in Maryland and Victoria identified more heroin-related deaths under their own definitions than a search of certificate text or national heroin codes. Morphine recorded instead of heroin, general drug wording and coding or registration issues contributed, but the comparisons do not validate a universal rate of deaths caused by heroin. An England and Wales projection addresses a different quantity: combined heroin/morphine deaths, not heroin misnamed as morphine. In Maryland in 2012–2015, the authors' search of the state's medical-examiner certificates found heroin named in 1,130 overdose deaths. A protocol developed by state agencies identified 2,182 using certificate text, toxicology and scene evidence: heroin on the certificate, a heroin-specific metabolite in tests, morphine with quinine, or morphine/unspecified certification together with scene evidence suggesting heroin. It excluded cases whose scene notes suggested prescription morphine. Because it retained every certificate naming heroin, it could only add heroin assignments. The 1,052 additions had morphine certified in 804 cases, no specific drug in 193 and another substance in 55. Certificates named heroin in 51.8% of protocol-defined deaths (95% interval 49.7–53.9), from 45.7% in 2012 to 56.3% in 2015, and less often among people aged 55 or older (41.9%), women (35.1%) and non-Hispanic Black women (25.9%). The authors acknowledge that some added cases, including some of the 55, may not have been heroin-related (Horon et al., 2018). In Victoria, Australia, in 2012–2013, the authors applied their earlier heroin-attribution model to closed coronial files, using toxicology plus circumstances, clinical and pathological evidence in the context of cause of death. It selected 243 deaths, with the heroin-specific marker in 180; the remaining 63 relied on morphine findings and investigative evidence (editors' subtraction). Of those selected, 235 were toxicity deaths and eight were misadventure deaths after heroin intoxication. Those eight are outside the national poisoning/dependence underlying-cause definition described in this comparison, so not every difference is a recording error. National data held 165 deaths with the heroin code, 161 inside the model-defined group and four judged coincidental by the model; 82 of the 243 lacked the heroin code, a net difference of 78 between totals. The Victorian attribution groups counted heroin named either in the cause of death or in the NCIS object-causing-death field. Of 191 toxicity deaths attributed to heroin on that basis, 37 lacked its code. The authors describe generic certification with drugs named only in the object field, morphine written as the cause with heroin only as the object, and complications listed first. They do not print a cross-tabulation separating wording issues from late registration in these groups. Of 39 deaths attributed to morphine or another opioid, 34 lacked the heroin code; all five generic-toxicity deaths lacked it. Twenty model-selected deaths had no code at all, which the authors judged most reasonably due to late initial registration and no coding assessment, not simply certificate wording. Since the study years, associated-cause toxicity codes have also become subject to revision when new information arrives, limiting application to newer statistics (Stam et al., 2019). In England and Wales in 2011–2022, ONS counted 13,471 deaths naming heroin or morphine in a cause-of-death field on the Record of Inquest. NPSUM's coroner reports and toxicology reports identified a further share with an ambiguous drug cause in which a consulting toxicologist implicated heroin/morphine: 29% in 2011 and 36% in 2022, the endpoint years rather than a range across all years. Applying those shares nationally, without linking individual records, projected 20,323 combined heroin/morphine deaths (95% interval 19,382–21,358), about 51% above the ONS count (editors' calculation). These intervals address sampling error in the programme's shares, not the assumption that those shares represent all cases. The median number of drugs detected in programme heroin/morphine deaths rose from four to six; detection is not proof that every drug caused death (Chen et al., 2025). A scoping review reports further comparisons second-hand. In Allegheny County in 2008–2010, heroin-involved deaths rose from 171 to 245 after review, while morphine-involved deaths fell from 132 to 41 and codeine-involved deaths from 34 to five; the decreases exceed the heroin increase, so these cannot be read as a one-for-one transfer between exclusive groups. In New York City in 2006–2010, 84 of 118 deaths certified as acute opiate intoxication were attributed to heroin. In SUDORS data for 38 states and Washington DC in 2018–2019, 44.2% of probable and 52.6% of suspected heroin deaths had only morphine on the certificate; enhanced definitions raised the heroin share from 80.2% to 93.3%. These primary studies were not read here, and their enhanced categories are not an independent test of true causal attribution (Gutkind et al., 2025). Heroin is rapidly converted to 6-acetylmorphine and then morphine; the specific marker may be absent after delayed death or change in stored specimens, so morphine after death can have several origins (Stam et al., 2019, describing earlier literature). National statistics also warn that a morphine mention may reflect heroin rather than direct morphine use (Garnett et al., 2026). A US medical-examiners' position paper treats 6-acetylmorphine as sufficient evidence of heroin without an attached citation; for a morphine-to-codeine ratio above one as possible evidence of heroin use it cites three empirical studies, but does not report the rule's diagnostic accuracy. Those studies were not independently read here (Davis et al., 2020). The Maryland and Victorian reference definitions were not validated against an independent causal standard, and the English and Welsh estimate is unlinked and combines two drugs. These historical findings cannot specify a current heroin-caused-death miss rate everywhere. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: Do official counts miss heroin deaths? In Maryland and Victoria, closer file reviews linked more deaths to heroin than certificate text or national codes did. Heroin turns into morphine in the body, and some records said morphine or mixed drugs instead. In Maryland, certificates named heroin in about 52 out of 100 deaths the fuller protocol linked to heroin. In Victoria, about 34 out of 100 model-selected deaths lacked the heroin code; a few coded as heroin were judged to involve it only by chance. The model also included some deaths outside the national poisoning definition. The reviews used their own rules, with no independent check of whether heroin caused each death. In England and Wales, a separate estimate suggests about half as many again as counted, but it combines heroin and morphine and does not match each death across the lists. These are different comparisons, not one missing-death rate.
set.magnitude: Maryland 2012–2015 (Horon et al., 2018; authors' certificate-text search versus enhanced protocol): 1,130 deaths with heroin on the certificate against 2,182 by the enhanced protocol (28.6% and 55.1% of 3,957 overdose deaths, a total not defined in the paper); added 1,052: morphine certified 804, no specific drug 193, other substance 55; certificates named heroin in 51.8% (49.7–53.9) of protocol deaths, 45.7% (2012) to 56.3% (2015); 41.9% at 55 or older, 35.1% of women, 25.9% (18.5–33.3) of non-Hispanic Black women. Victoria 2012–2013 (Stam et al., 2019): 243 model-defined deaths (235 toxicity, 8 misadventure outside the selected national underlying-cause definition; 6-acetylmorphine in 180) against 165 with the heroin code; code missing from 82 (34%, editors' arithmetic); 4 coded deaths judged coincidental; heroin attributed in cause-of-death or NCIS object field, coded 154 of 191; morphine or other opioid certified 5 of 39 coded; generic 0 of 5; 20 with no code, authors' likely late-initial-registration explanation. England and Wales 2011–2022 (Chen et al., 2025; unlinked projection): combined heroin/morphine ONS 13,471 against 20,323 projected (95% interval 19,382–21,358) (about 51% more, editors' calculation); 2011 574 against 813 (95% CI 767–868); 2022 1,264 against 1,980 (95% interval 1,894–2,074). Second-hand (Gutkind et al., 2025): Allegheny County heroin 171 to 245, morphine 132 to 41, codeine 34 to 5; New York City 84 of 118 opiate-intoxication deaths attributed to heroin. SUDORS 38 states and DC, 2018–2019, second-hand in Gutkind: morphine-only certificate wording in 44.2% of probable and 52.6% of suspected heroin deaths; enhanced heroin share 80.2% to 93.3%. Reference standards unvalidated; no intervals for Victorian counts. Chen reports Wilson intervals for projections, covering sampling error only; Table 1 values used where the text differs.

set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: Maryland and Victorian reference definitions are not independently validated causal standards. They combine toxicological markers and investigative evidence; Stam evaluates them in the context of cause of death, so it is too absolute to say no causal judgment occurred. Who reviewed and blinding to codes are not described in the inherited Horon extraction or supplied Stam methods (cards moderate). Victoria also uses a broader misadventure definition and has late-registration/coding limits. England/Wales is an unlinked combined heroin/morphine projection (high); its sampling intervals exclude representation/attribution assumptions. A stricter causal or harmonised definition could change the gaps.
set.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: Not downgraded: same-file heroin comparisons in Maryland and Victoria and second-hand US comparisons point toward incomplete heroin attribution. They do not share a common magnitude or all measure one mechanism: England/Wales measures combined heroin/morphine ambiguous wording, not substitution of morphine for heroin.
set.grade.domains.indirectness.note: Rated as worded: each setting, period and reference is identified; historical file-review findings, second-hand review summaries and combined heroin/morphine projections are distinguished. Presence, use and causal attribution are not treated as equivalent, and definition/registration changes limit application to current statistics.
set.grade.reasoning: Descriptive claim starts low, never upgraded (METHODS §6.3); one downgrade for risk of bias gives very low. Maryland and Victoria compare the same files under different rules, the most direct comparisons here, but their reference definitions are unvalidated. The broader Victorian misadventure definition accounts for some discrepancy by design; its code revision process later changed. Chen is a different, unlinked combined heroin/morphine outcome. Horon appears inside Gutkind and is counted once; county and SUDORS results are explicitly second-hand, not newly verified primary evidence. Replicated concerns direction of incomplete heroin attribution across independent settings, not an agreed true heroin-caused death miss rate. Reverse differences are retained: four coded Victorian cases judged coincidental; Maryland retained every heroin-naming certificate and could only add.
